title: Try a Lot of Stuff and Keep What Works
hook: Chalk arrows drying on wet pavement turn Emily's market into a disciplined test.
counterintuition: More experiments do not mean more learning. Without a measure that belongs to the core, variation teaches the team to survive variety instead of improving what the organization promised.
tryThisNow: Pick one method you use. Write three variations, the one measure tied to the core, and the date you will keep one and kill the rest.
keyTakeaway: Try many bounded variations, measure them against the core purpose, keep what proves itself, and drop the rest before experimentation becomes drift.

breakdown.fastRead:
Chalk arrows dry on wet pavement before the farmers market opens. Emily has three stall layouts for three Wednesdays, not a pile of random gimmicks. She will count dwell time and vendor sales, then check whether local producers, not resellers, benefit.

The institution does not have to predict the winning method if it can test many methods and keep the one that proves itself. The core chooses what counts as proof.

Variation needs a judge before novelty becomes drift.
breakdown.deepRead:
Trying a lot of stuff works only when the stuff is bounded and the standard is clear. Without a standard, experiments become trend-chasing. With a standard, variation becomes learning. The institution can move without losing itself because feedback is measured against the core.

Emily's market is not testing whatever might draw a crowd. It is testing layouts that help local producers meet buyers. If a layout increases foot traffic by adding reseller booths, it fails even if the street looks busier. If another layout slows shoppers near farm stalls and lifts vendor sales, it stays.

Keep what works means define works first.

Nicolas learns the same thing in a physical therapy clinic. Three discharge formats sit on the treatment table: a dense packet, a checklist, and a photo card. His favorite is the packet because it feels complete. Follow-up adherence says otherwise. Knee patients use the photo card, flare up less, and return with clearer questions. The clinic keeps the method patients actually use.

The limit is patience. Experiments need enough time to teach, but not so much time that every weak variation earns a permanent home. Set a kill date before the test begins. The ending is what turns a trial into evidence instead of another habit to defend.
breakdown.fullRead:
"Which pilot made people show up at the council meeting?" Anna asks, with listener notes beside an attendance sheet. The most popular radio segment has the biggest audience spike. It also sends nobody toward public life. The quieter explainer brings fewer listeners and more people into the council room.

That is the discipline of experimentation inside a purpose. The station can try new formats without surrendering public-service reporting, because the test is not raw popularity. The test is whether the format helps listeners act like citizens. Once that measure is visible, Anna can cancel the most popular pilot without treating experimentation as failure.

What would you keep if the prettiest number stopped being the right number? That question separates learning from fashion. A team can test apps, routes, formats, reminders, layouts, scripts, and schedules. It still needs one core measure that says which result matters.

Diego runs a quieter version in bike-share maintenance. Rain beads on laminated route cards taped to mechanic vans. For two weeks each neighborhood gets a different routing pattern. The winning route is not the one mechanics like best or the one that looks neatest on a map. It is the route that reduces repeat broken-bike pickups at the same docks. The method survives because commuters regain trust.

Ingrid's language school learns through loss. Refund forms stack under three placement rubrics. The written test is fastest and easiest to schedule. The trial class is slower. For borderline adult learners, the trial class produces fewer refunds and less early embarrassment. Ingrid keeps the slower method where confidence is fragile and drops it where the written test already works.

This kind of adaptation requires emotional restraint. People attach themselves to ideas they proposed. Departments defend pilots because they gave up evenings to run them. Leaders protect experiments because public failure feels costly. The rule has to be stated before the test: the variation that serves the core stays, the others leave with thanks.

There is also a false version of keeping what works. A tactic may work by damaging the thing you meant to protect. A radio stunt may raise listeners while hollowing civic trust. A market gimmick may increase traffic while crowding out local farmers. A pharmacy app may look modern while transplant patients miss pickups. The feedback has to be tied to the purpose, or the institution will retain the wrong success.

Lin sees the point in the refill labels. Phone calls, postcards, and app reminders are sorted into three colored trays for separate transplant-patient cohorts. The app looks clean. The low-tech call script reduces missed pickups. Lin keeps the call script because immunosuppressant adherence, not technical elegance, is the work.

Learning organizations are not lucky because they guess better. They are durable because they test honestly, keep selectively, and let weak methods die.

examples.title: Emily chalks three market paths

planSpec.domain: urban farmers market testing stall layouts while preserving local-producer standards
planSpec.audience: Emily, market manager with declining Wednesday traffic
planSpec.stakes: vendors need footfall, but the market cannot become a flea market to chase crowds
planSpec.requiredBeat: Emily chalks three stall patterns over three Wednesdays, counts dwell time and vendor sales, then keeps the layout that helps local produce without adding reseller booths

examples.scenario: Chalk arrows dry on wet pavement before vendors arrive for the first of three Wednesdays. Emily predicts the widest aisle will win. She counts dwell time and sales without adding reseller booths. By week three, the diagonal layout keeps shoppers near local produce longest, and Emily has to choose evidence over the layout she expected to love. A cheese vendor has marked slow sales on a receipt, so Emily treats the chalk arrows as a producer test, not a crowd-control exercise.
examples.whatToDo: Test three stall patterns, count dwell time and vendor sales, and keep the layout that helps local producers without changing the market's standard.
examples.whyItMatters: The market needs variation inside its identity. A crowd boost that weakens local-producer standards would be drift, not learning.

examples.title: Nicolas keeps the photo card

planSpec.domain: physical therapy clinic testing discharge instructions for knee patients
planSpec.audience: Nicolas, clinic owner frustrated by recurring setbacks
planSpec.stakes: patients keep returning with avoidable flare-ups after unclear home routines
planSpec.requiredBeat: At 4:20 p.m., Nicolas compares three instruction formats by follow-up adherence, then keeps the photo card that patients actually use

examples.scenario: At 4:20 p.m., Nicolas lines three discharge packets along a treatment table: dense notes, a checklist, and a photo card. He expected clinicians to prefer the detailed packet. Follow-up adherence says knee patients use the photo card. By the next staff meeting, the favorite packet is gone for routine cases. One patient has returned with swelling after losing the old packet, which makes the adherence result feel like care evidence.
examples.whatToDo: Compare the three instruction formats by patient adherence, not clinician preference. Keep the photo card where it reduces avoidable flare-ups.
examples.whyItMatters: Instructions work only when patients use them at home. Feedback from adherence beats the format that feels most complete in the clinic.

examples.title: Anna cancels the popular pilot

planSpec.domain: public radio station experimenting with local news formats without abandoning public-service reporting
planSpec.audience: Anna, program director watching younger listeners leave
planSpec.stakes: chasing attention could dilute the station's civic role
planSpec.requiredBeat: "Which pilot made people show up at the council meeting?" Anna asks, then cancels the most popular segment because it did not serve the core

examples.scenario: Anna points to the council agenda on the public radio conference table and asks which pilot actually moved listeners into the room. Three pilots ran all month. The funniest segment won downloads but produced no civic turnout. Anna must decide whether popularity wins or the quieter public-service format stays. A reporter has left a council agenda on the table, making Anna compare downloads with civic action before renewing any format.
examples.whatToDo: Judge the pilots by the public-service test, not downloads alone. Cancel the popular segment if it does not move listeners toward civic action.
examples.whyItMatters: Experimentation needs a core measure. Popularity can be useful, but it cannot define success for a station built around public service.

examples.title: Diego keeps the repeat-pickup route

planSpec.domain: bike-share maintenance crew testing repair-routing cards across neighborhoods
planSpec.audience: Diego, field operations lead with uneven bike availability
planSpec.stakes: commuters lose trust when docks are full of broken bikes in the same areas
planSpec.requiredBeat: Diego tapes different routing cards to mechanic vans for two weeks, then keeps the route that reduces repeat broken-bike pickups

examples.scenario: Rainwater beads on a laminated van route card while Diego tapes the second version to a mechanic's dashboard. For two weeks, each neighborhood gets a different routing card. The crews prefer the shortest loop. Diego has to choose the route that reduces repeat broken-bike pickups, even though it feels less tidy. A commuter complaint from the same dock is taped near the van keys, so Diego follows repeat failure instead of route neatness.
examples.whatToDo: Run the route cards for two weeks and keep the one that lowers repeat pickups at the same docks. Let commuter reliability decide.
examples.whyItMatters: A neat route is not the core outcome. The useful test is whether riders stop finding the same broken bikes in the same places.

examples.title: Ingrid drops the fast test

planSpec.domain: language school trying placement interviews, written tests, and trial classes for adult learners
planSpec.audience: Ingrid, academic coordinator defending student confidence
planSpec.stakes: wrong placement makes adults quit before learning begins
planSpec.requiredBeat: It took Ingrid one refund report to keep the trial class method and drop the faster written test for borderline students

examples.scenario: Ingrid opens the language school refund report beside three placement rubrics in her office. Interviews, written exams, and trial classes all ran for the same intake month. The written test was fastest, but borderline adults placed by trial class quit less often, so Ingrid has to choose the slower method where confidence is most fragile. A refund email from a borderline student sits beside the rubrics, turning the slower trial class into confidence protection.
examples.whatToDo: Use refund and placement data to split the methods. Keep trial classes for borderline students and drop the faster written test where it damages confidence.
examples.whyItMatters: The school is testing for fit that adults can survive. Speed is useful only when it does not place learners into early failure.

examples.title: Lin keeps the call script

planSpec.domain: specialty pharmacy testing refill reminders for transplant patients under strict adherence rules
planSpec.audience: Lin, pharmacist responsible for missed-dose risk
planSpec.stakes: missed immunosuppressant doses can threaten a transplant
planSpec.requiredBeat: You watch Lin test phone, postcard, and app reminders on separate refill cohorts, then keep the low-tech call script because it reduces missed pickups

examples.scenario: You watch Lin sort refill labels in the specialty pharmacy at 7:30 a.m., using three colored trays for transplant patients: phone, postcard, app. The missed pickup log sits beside the labels. Everyone expects the app to win, but Lin has to choose the low-tech call script after it reduces missed immunosuppressant pickups in the cohort that needed the most help. A transplant nurse has circled two missed pickups on the log, so Lin keeps the call script where risk is highest.
examples.whatToDo: Test phone, postcard, and app reminders in separate cohorts, then keep the reminder that lowers missed pickups for transplant patients.
examples.whyItMatters: The core outcome is adherence, not modernity. The method that protects transplant patients stays, even when it looks less impressive.

questions.prompt: When five onboarding pilots launch without a shared definition of speed, retention, support load, or trust, what is the main risk?
choices: They will offend people whose ideas lose and make future pilot teams less willing to try
They will learn too slowly because five pilots split attention across too many formats
They may keep the most exciting variation instead of the one that serves the core
questions.explanation: Variation needs a judge. Without a core measure, excitement or politics can decide what survives.

questions.prompt: For a market layout test, one option restores foot traffic by adding reseller booths that crowd out local farmers. How should success be measured?
choices: By which layout vendors say feels most energetic and easiest to manage during rush periods
By total visitor count plus whether the larger crowd returns on the next market day
By dwell time and sales for local producers within the market standard
questions.explanation: The test must preserve the local-producer core. Visitor count alone could reward drift away from the market's purpose.

questions.prompt: Patients follow a photo card more reliably than the clinic owner's preferred detailed packet after knee discharge. What should he keep?
choices: The detailed packet because it contains more information
Both formats for every patient to avoid conflict
The photo card for routine cases because adherence is the relevant feedback
questions.explanation: The useful feedback is patient adherence at home. Completeness in the clinic matters less if patients do not use the packet.

questions.prompt: One radio pilot wins downloads, while a quieter format sends more listeners to council meetings. Which pilot fits the station's purpose?
choices: The quieter format, if public-service reporting is the core
The download winner may deserve priority because public-service work needs audience scale to matter
Neither, because experiments should not affect news formats
questions.explanation: The right measure depends on the purpose. If civic action is the core, raw downloads cannot be the sole test.

questions.prompt: Two repair routes compete: crews prefer the shortest loop, but the longer loop reduces repeat broken-bike pickups. Which route should stay?
choices: The shortest route because crews will follow it more happily
The route that reduces repeat pickups at unreliable docks
A new route chosen by whichever mechanic has seniority
questions.explanation: The core outcome is rider trust through reliable docks. Crew preference matters, but it does not outrank the measured pickup problem.

questions.prompt: When teachers want to keep all three classroom pilots because each took evenings to prepare, what discipline prevents permanent clutter?
choices: More appreciation for creative staff, paired with a review of which pilots teachers enjoyed
More time before judgment, since classroom pilots often need a full term to show results
A kill date and a rule for retaining only what proves itself
questions.explanation: Experiments need gratitude and endings. Without a kill date, weak variations become permanent clutter.

questions.prompt: The pharmacy app looks modern, but phone reminders reduce missed transplant-medication pickups. What should the pharmacist do?
choices: Keep the phone script where adherence improves
Switch everyone to the app for consistency
Use postcards because they cost less
questions.explanation: Adherence is the core measure. The less modern method wins if it better protects transplant patients from missed doses.

questions.prompt: When a restaurant discount raises traffic but trains customers to ignore the local-sourcing promise, how should leaders evaluate it?
choices: Keep it because traffic proves the test worked
Reject or redesign it because the apparent win damages the core
Extend it for six months to collect more data
questions.explanation: A tactic can work on one number while harming the purpose. The core measure has to veto that false success.

questions.prompt: Pricing, service scripts, and schedules are open to experiment, but staff fear identity drift. Which setup best addresses that fear?
choices: Allow only one safe pilot per year so staff can see that identity still matters
Define the core measure first, then test many bounded methods against it
Let departments choose experiments freely and compare results in a shared review later
questions.explanation: Bounded variation with a core measure lets methods change while identity holds. Avoiding experiments or scattering them both miss that discipline.

reviewCards.front: What must be defined before trying many variations?
reviewCards.back: Define what counts as working in terms of the core purpose. Without that judge, experiments become fashion, politics, or noise.

reviewCards.front: Why can the most popular pilot still lose?
reviewCards.back: Popularity may not serve the core. Keep the pilot that advances the purpose, not the one with the prettiest surface metric.

reviewCards.front: What does a kill date do for experimentation?
reviewCards.back: It prevents weak variations from becoming permanent because people worked hard on them. Tests need endings so the institution can retain selectively.

reviewCards.front: How can experimentation protect identity without threatening it?
reviewCards.back: Run many bounded methods against one clear core measure. The method can change because the purpose decides what survives.

reviewCards.front: Traffic rises while the core weakens. What kind of feedback is that?
reviewCards.back: False feedback. It rewards a visible metric while damaging the promise that metric was supposed to serve; keep the method only if the core measure improves too.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Design experiments with a retention rule. The skill is to vary methods, define the core measure in advance, and keep only what proves itself by that measure. Honest killing is part of institutional learning.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you test multiple formats, then name the core measure before the first pilot launches.
If staff prefer one variation, then compare that preference with the outcome the process exists to protect.
If a test improves a surface metric, then check whether the core promise improved too before retaining it.
If an experiment begins, then set the kill date and owner for the retention decision.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tomorrow, choose one method and draft three bounded variations. Add one core measure and the date when two variations will be retired.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one active experiment. Decide what evidence would make you keep it, change it, or kill it, then record the decision.
implementationPlan.title: Testing experiments with retention rules
